title: Safety-net participation was associated with greater social stigma but not different government perceptions in a California low-income caregiver sample
source_unit: Low-income California caregivers of young children surveyed during the first COVID-19 pandemic year, with SNAP and EITC participation measures

observations.period: August 2020–May 2021; Health Affairs Scholar article published December 2023 / Volume 2 Issue 1 (2024)

denominator.unit: caregivers of young children in the ACCESS survey; analytic subsamples 489 SNAP-eligible and 326 EITC-eligible respondents

snap_social_stigma.value: OR 1.24 (95% CI 1.05–1.47) for greater reported social stigma
snap_social_stigma.unit: adjusted odds ratio, SNAP participants versus eligible nonparticipants

eitc_social_stigma.value: OR 1.39 (95% CI 1.05–1.84) for greater reported social stigma
eitc_social_stigma.unit: adjusted odds ratio, EITC recipients versus eligible nonrecipients

government_perceptions.value: no statistically significant difference for SNAP participation or EITC receipt

program_stigma_and_discrimination.value: no overall difference; among food-insecure respondents, SNAP participation was additionally associated with program stigma and discrimination

observations.method: Health Affairs Scholar study of the ACCESS cross-sectional survey, using multivariable logistic regression among low-income California caregivers and separate SNAP-eligible and EITC-eligible analytic samples to relate participation/receipt to government perceptions, social and program stigma, and discrimination.
observations.uncertainty: This is a cross-sectional, convenience/snowball-recruited California sample during COVID-19, not a causal program effect or national estimate. Reverse causation and unmeasured confounding are possible; social stigma is not the same as institutional distrust, approval, or political action.
observations.subgroup: Low-income caregivers of children ages 0–8; food-insecure SNAP-eligible respondents formed a nonrepresentative sensitivity subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: Participation may be selected by prior stigma, hardship, service contact, or discrimination rather than causing stigma. The absence of a government-perception difference does not establish positive trust, and reported stigma may affect take-up without producing turnout or exit.

related_sources.claim: Health Affairs Scholar DOI and publication metadata identify the article.

boundary: This is a California cross-sectional association between safety-net participation and stigma/government-perception measures, not a causal trust effect, national estimate, or completed take-up-to-action pathway.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Oxford Academic article-minimal page downloaded and hashed; title, publication date, sample, analytic subsamples, odds ratios, null government-perception result, food-insecurity subgroup, and cross-sectional limitations checked against the article text.
